title: Africa University
summary: Africa University thanks North Georgia congregations for supporting the Africa University Fund and reports a year of strong growth. In June 2025 AU graduated its largest class ever, and the fall brought its most diverse incoming class. The report urges churches to maintain AUF support and become Keystone Congregations.
contentMd:
Africa University (AU) reports strong 2025 growth: it graduated its largest class ever (622 students from 20 African countries) and welcomed its most diverse incoming class (students from 30 nations). Students study in four colleges, a law school, and two institutes on a debt-free campus. Highlights include a self-funded solar plant supplying 100% of campus electricity, a new collaboration with the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, expanded applied-research partnership with UMC Global Ministries on agriculture and malaria, media training with United Methodist Communications, and the law school's moot court team representing Africa at a 2026 world competition in the UK.

AU urges congregations to maintain Africa University Fund support at the 2016 budget level, work toward 100% funding, and consider becoming a "Keystone Congregation" by committing $7,000 annually to support one undergraduate student.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 100 (Africa University)

title: Candler School of Theology
summary: Candler School of Theology, an official UMC seminary, reports a diverse student body and continued commitment to Wesleyan and ecumenical formation for ministry in the 21st century.
contentMd: Candler School of Theology, an official seminary of The United Methodist Church, maintains a strong Methodist presence among students, faculty, and staff while holding to the Wesleyan value of ecumenical openness. Enrollment is 507 students from 11 countries, 42 states, 45 denominations, and 34 United Methodist annual conferences, with 50% persons of color. Candler frames this diversity as a blessing that enriches community life and provides the context for training in relevant ministry for the 21st century—ministry that cultivates community across difference and welcomes all.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 101 (Candler School of Theology)

title: Episcopacy Committee Report: Georgia Area
summary: The North and South Georgia Episcopacy Committees celebrate Bishop Robin Dease's ministry across the One Georgia Area. The report notes her healing presence after disaffiliation, the Thriving Leadership Initiative, and the submission of the Georgia Unification plan in March 2026.
contentMd:
The chairs of the South Georgia and North Georgia Episcopacy Committees (Melissa Traver and Robert S. King) report on their Disciplinary task of supporting and resourcing Bishop Robin Dease. They celebrate her ministry across the One Georgia Area, riding the circuit to preach and worship, and providing a healing presence to congregations, mergers, and new church starts after the disaffiliation season. She has served on a Council of Bishops steering committee for covenant support groups.

The Bishop's Thriving Leadership Initiative continues to engage clergy, laity, and congregations, including multi-ethnic and new-church-start contexts. After eighteen months of discernment, the North and South Georgia conferences submitted their unification report in March 2026 (georgiaumc.org/unification-plan), the work of twenty working groups. The report also notes the December 2025 retirement of administrative assistant Renee Farrar and the welcome of Beth Blakeley in January 2026.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 102 (Episcopacy Committee Report: Georgia Area)

title: Faith Connection Federal Credit Union
summary: Faith Connection Federal Credit Union, founded in 1960 to serve Georgia Methodist pastors, now has over 3,000 members across the Georgia/Florida/southern Alabama connection. The report includes a 2025 financial statement showing total assets of about $32.1 million.
contentMd:
Faith Connection Federal Credit Union began in 1960 serving North and South Georgia UMC pastors; its charter has expanded to clergy, staff, and laity across Georgia, Florida, and southern Alabama, with over 3,000 members. It reports steady growth in credit card, auto, and home equity loans, with credit card balances near $3 million, auto loans of $7 million, and $2.5 million in secured home equity loans. The credit union gave back to eight annual conferences through scholarships, sponsorships, and donations (including UMCOR and Methodist children's homes). Every United Methodist is eligible for membership.

Financial Report (103.a): As of 12/31/2025, total assets were $32,149,377.30 (down from $33,286,993.97 in 2024); total liabilities $278,108.51; total equity $31,871,268.79; net income $36,987.95. Members' shares totaled $28,491,217.91. Chair: Garth Duke Barton.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 103 (Faith Connection Federal Credit Union, incl. 103.a Financial Report)

title: Gammon Theological Seminary
summary: Gammon, the UMC's only Historically Black Theological Institution, reports progress toward independent accreditation, enrollment of 41 students, and major grant support for its "Gammon 3.0" expansion.
contentMd:
Gammon Theological Seminary remains the only Historically Black Theological Institution (HBTI) of The United Methodist Church. After launching an independent Master of Divinity program in 2024, Gammon hosted its initial SACSCOC site visit in October 2025, receiving affirmation of 93% compliance, with final review pending the June 2026 SACSCOC board meeting; it aims for full ATS accreditation by December 2027. As of Spring 2026 Gammon enrolls 41 students (10 new, 31 continuing), with about 73% United Methodist-affiliated.

Fund development included a three-year $975,000 capacity-building grant from GBHEM, a $375,000 grant from the Pitts Foundation for Phase III renovations, a $250,000 scholarship grant from the SOMA Foundation, and the launch of the "Become 1 of 1 Million" endowed scholarship campaign. President & CEO: Candace M. Lewis.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 104 (Gammon Theological Seminary)

title: Georgia Pastors' School
summary: Georgia Pastors' School met July 14–17, 2025, at Epworth By The Sea under the theme "Reigniting Joy." Bishop Dease preached, and worship offerings of $2,191.86 went to UMCOR for Texas flood victims.
contentMd:
Georgia Pastors' School convened July 14–17, 2025, at Epworth By The Sea on St. Simons Island under the theme "Reigniting Joy," aiming to refresh clergy after a difficult season in the UMC. Bishop Robin Dease preached the first night and celebrated Holy Communion on the last day; guest teachers were Candace Lewis (Gammon) and Matt Rawle (Asbury UMC, Louisiana). The week included worship, teaching, shared meals, and activities for spouses, children, and youth.

Attendance included 81 active clergy, 12 commuting clergy, 4 lay ministers, 25 retired clergy, 26 spouses, 19 children, and 9 youth. Worship offerings totaled $2,191.86, designated to UMCOR for Texas flood victims. The next school is July 13–16, 2026, featuring Tod Bolsinger and Amber Lowe-Woodfork.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 105 (Georgia Pastors' School)

title: Hinton Rural Life Center
summary: Hinton Rural Life Center, a mission and retreat center in western North Carolina, reports extensive 2025 volunteer service and rural outreach serving 1,287 neighbors in Appalachia.
contentMd:
Hinton Rural Life Center, a mission outreach and retreat center of the SEJ in the southwest corner of North Carolina, serves individuals, congregations, and rural communities through retreats, education, and missional outreach. In 2025, 1,186 volunteers served over 23,755 hours (valued at $826,436). The center hosted 365 confirmands in Theotokos Confirmation Retreats, 664 mission participants on home repairs and community projects, and 27 adults in its new Boomers on Outreach Mission (BOOM) initiative.

Through year-round Mission Outreach, Hinton served 1,287 Appalachian neighbors: 232 Safe & Healthy Home repair projects on 58 homes, 805 loads of firewood (valued at $161,000), Christmas gifts for 511 children, and a rural poverty simulation for 830 participants. CEO & President: Dr. Jacqueline Gottlieb.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 106 (Hinton Rural Life Center)

title: Lake Junaluska
summary: Lake Junaluska Assembly reports on its Sharing Our Gifts Capital Campaign (now in its fifth and final year, with over $16 million committed), a 2025 financial surplus, and upcoming 2026 worship and ministry programs.
contentMd:
Lake Junaluska Assembly reports on its mission of Christian hospitality. The Sharing Our Gifts Capital Campaign is in its fifth and final year, with more than $16 million committed; priorities include preserving the lake and dam, enhancements around the Cross, recreation-area revitalization, youth and family housing, and Stuart Auditorium improvements. Lake Junaluska concluded 2025 with a financial surplus invested in living wages for staff, and the Annual Fund exceeded its goal for the seventh consecutive year.

Upcoming 2026 programming includes the Summer Worship and Theologian in Residence series (June 28–August 2), the Festival of Wisdom and Grace (August 17–21), and the 37th Choir Music Weekend (October 16–18). Encounter confirmation weekends welcomed nearly 500 youth over two weekends under the theme "Unshakable Faith."
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 107 (Lake Junaluska)

title: Georgia Professional Administrators of the UM Connectional Structure
summary: PAUMCS, established in 1982 under GCFA, provides administrative professionals across United Methodism with fellowship, professional development, and certification. The Georgia Chapter hopes to revive its in-person conference.
contentMd:
The Professional Administrators of the United Methodist Connectional Structure (PAUMCS) was established in 1982 under the General Council on Finance and Administration to provide members fellowship, individual growth, professional development, continuing education, and spiritual enrichment (Book of Discipline ¶807.19). PAUMCS members serve in local churches, district offices, extension ministries, agencies, and annual conferences. National membership is open to paid administrative professionals and requires certification offered through GCFA, with continuing-education credits to maintain it.

The Georgia Chapter, which includes the North and South Georgia conferences, has not held an in-person conference in recent years but hopes to revive and flourish again. Submitted by LouAnn P. McLain, GA PAUMCS Immediate Past President.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 108 (Professional Administrators of the UM Connectional Structure)

title: Barnes Evaluation and Administrative Team
summary: The Barnes Evaluation and Administrative Team (BEAT) reports a sixth year of grant-making for innovative ministries. Since 2020 BEAT has funded over $5.7 million to 114 recipients; in 2025 it awarded 18 grants totaling $1,084,271.
contentMd:
The Barnes Evaluation and Administrative Team (BEAT) reports its sixth year of funding innovative missions and ministries. Since its 2020 inception, BEAT has funded more than $5.7 million to 114 boards, agencies, churches, and districts across the conference's five districts. It hosted two BEAT Academy training events (September 2025 and February 2026). In 2026 BEAT moved from three funding windows to two (April and October); annual funding equals 5% of the fund's three-year average end-of-year balance.

In 2025 the funding allocation was $1,493,000: twelve grants totaling $721,023 were approved in the May window and six grants totaling $363,248 in the November window, for 18 grants totaling $1,084,271. In 2026, BEAT has $1,559,900 available. Co-chairs: Rev. Dr. Orlando Evans and Kim Walls Powell.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 200 (Barnes Evaluation and Administrative Team)

title: Center for Clergy Excellence
summary: The Center for Clergy Excellence supports credentialing, cultivation, and sustaining of clergy. It reports Ministerial Education Fund scholarships, candidacy growth, clergy renewal retreats, and includes subsections from the Board of Ordained Ministry and the Orders of Deacons and Elders.
contentMd:
The Center for Clergy Excellence supports credentialing, cultivation, and sustaining of all elders, deacons, associate members, provisional members, and local pastors, working with the bishop, cabinet, Board of Ordained Ministry, and five District Committees on Ordained Ministry. In 2025–2026 the Ministerial Education Fund supported 16 candidates with $75,000 toward master's-level education and 28 local pastors with $21,000 for Course of Study; 45 Certified Candidates are in the credentialing process. In 2026, 7 candidates will be commissioned and 6 ordained. Clergy renewal offerings included the 8-Year Renewal (32 clergy), Clergy Days Away at Camp Glisson (68) and Ignatius House (41), Enneagram studies, and Group Spiritual Direction. Director: P. Alice Rogers.

**201.a Board of Ordained Ministry:** The BOM interviews candidates for provisional membership and ordination, supports the Residency in Ministry process, and oversees continuing education. In September 2025 it approved revised educational requirements allowing fully online degrees from 13 approved UM schools of theology, aligning with University Senate policy; it will add a 2027 interview question on Artificial Intelligence. Chair: Josh Roberts.

**201.b Fellowship of Local Pastors and Associate Members:** Anchored in Matthew 25:37–40, the Fellowship gives thanks for ministry to "the least of these" and recognizes those who completed Course of Study, Advanced Course of Study, and seminary. Chair: YoLanda Jones-Colton.

**201.c Order of Deacons:** Deacons are called to a lifetime ministry of Word, Service, Compassion, and Justice as bridge-builders between church and world; 2026 marks 30 years since the 1996 establishment of the Order. Chair: Montana Hamby.

**201.d Order of Elders:** Committed to Order, Service, Word, and Table, the Order embraces the 2026 conference theme "Unto the Least of These" and supports clergy retreat, renewal, and fellowship. Chairperson: M. Lavell Sanders.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 201 (Center for Clergy Excellence, incl. 201.a–d)

title: Conference Communications Office
summary: The Conference Communications Office handles internal and external communications via the website, e-newsletters, social media, and video. This year it focused on the unification effort and welcomed new communications director Meghan Walters.
contentMd:
The Conference Communications Office manages internal and external communications for the North Georgia Conference—online content, news and resources for leaders, the annual conference session, and media relationships. Over the past year it especially focused on the study and pursuit of unification with the South Georgia Conference. Key tools include the conference website (ngumc.org, up to 30,000 visitors monthly), the "Weekly Update" e-newsletter, and social media (Facebook, Instagram @NGUMC, Vimeo). The office also relates to United Methodist Communications.

Early this year the office bid farewell to longtime communications director Sybil Davidson, who took another denominational position, and welcomed Meghan Walters as the next director of communications.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 202 (Conference Communications Office)

title: Conference Statistician Team
summary: The Conference Statistician reports 2025 end-of-year figures: 401 churches, 196,836 members, average worship attendance of 38,896, with professions of faith and baptisms both up from 2024.
contentMd:
The Conference Statistician (Dana A. Everhart) and District Statisticians compiled the 2025 End of Year Report, framing the work theologically around 2 Corinthians 13. Key 2025 figures: 401 churches (down from 411 in 2024); 196,836 members (down from 203,358); average worship attendance of 38,896 (down from 39,218); professions of faith of 1,031 (up from 982); and baptisms of 1,241 (up from 1,186). The report attributes declines to a clearer post-disaffiliation picture and calls remaining members to evangelism and invitation.

All statistical data from 2002 to 2025 is available by church, district, and conference at ngumc.org/eoy, with year-to-year comparisons.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 203 (Conference Statistician)

title: NGC Housing and Homeless Council
summary: The Housing and Homeless Council supports congregations serving people experiencing poverty and homelessness through education, advocacy, and grants. In 2025 it awarded $100,400 in grants to 21 ministries, with the annual Homeless Offering raising $74,593.
contentMd:
The North Georgia Conference Housing and Homeless Council (HHC) supports congregations serving those experiencing poverty and homelessness through education, advocacy, and capital and operational grants. Citing HUD data of an estimated 12,290 people experiencing homelessness on a given night in Georgia, the Council awards grants twice a year. In 2025 it awarded $100,400 in grants to twenty-one ministries across all five districts (2025 grantees at nghhc.org/2025-grantees).

The annual Homeless Offering (fourth Sunday of February) raised $74,593 from 73 local churches in 2025—a 26.5% increase over 2024—with 100% returned to communities through grants; the balance of need was covered by the endowment. The Housing Trust Fund, invested with the Georgia United Methodist Foundation, ended the year valued at $1,902,429.72. Director: Stacey Rushing; Chair: Brian Hooker.

2025 capital grant recipients (204.a) included Clifton Sanctuary Ministries ($10,000), Family Promise Hall County ($10,000), Habitat for Humanity–DeKalb ($5,000), Helping Hands of Paulding County ($10,000), Impact 46 ($10,000), Ivy and Roses Community Fund ($5,000), Rainbow Community Center ($10,000), and Rainbow Village ($10,000).
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 204 (NGC Housing and Homeless Council, incl. 204.a Grant Report)

title: Director of Connectional Ministries
summary: The Director of Connectional Ministries reports on Regional Developers deployed through a Lilly Endowment Thriving Congregations grant, district trainings, and the growth of the Thriving Leadership Initiative. The report folds in the conference Safe Sanctuary policy.
contentMd:
Connectional Ministries focused on getting into churches and creating new ministry pathways. Five Regional Developers (RDs), funded through the Lilly Endowment's Thriving Congregations Initiative grant for the 24/25 and 25/26 conference years, built relationships in their assigned districts and focused on areas including Next Gen ministries, Black church development, discipleship and Fresh Expressions, Hispanic/Latine church development and immigration support, and the Thriving Leadership Initiative. The team offered coaching and trainings (church council, SPRC, trustees, finance, stewardship) and district-specific in-person events.

The Thriving Leadership Initiative (TLI) grew into a transformational learning community integrating clergy and laity through in-person events and monthly online Learning Labs on adaptive leadership, financial wellness, conflict transformation, discipleship, and community engagement. Submitted by Rev. Laurie Moeller.

The report also includes the conference Policy for Reducing the Risk of Abuse for Children, Youth, and Vulnerable Adults (Safe Sanctuary), which sets recruiting and screening standards (background checks, character references, minimum ages, six-month membership), mandatory training, two-adult supervision, and reporting procedures that follow Georgia law. Originally adopted in 1998, the policy was reviewed and updated for the 2026 session.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 300 (Director of Connectional Ministries, incl. Safe Sanctuary policy)

title: Connectional Ministries Team Report
summary: The Connectional Ministries Team (CMT) organizes its work around the Connectional Table's five areas of focus and three responsibilities (advocacy, discipleship, resources/stewardship). It evaluates grants and presents Church of Excellence Awards.
contentMd:
The Connectional Ministries Team (CMT) is a collection of ministry teams centered on the Connectional Table's five areas of focus: New Faith Opportunities & Communities, Scriptural Literacy & Imagination, Racial Justice & Healing, Health & Wellbeing, and Community Engagement. Its work is framed by three responsibilities: Advocacy, Discipleship, and Resources/Stewardship. CMT members participated in the Georgia Interfaith Public Policy Event at Oak Grove UMC and developed a discipleship resource page (ngumc.org/discipleship).

CMT evaluates grant applications from UM affiliates before they go to BEAT for final review, and it develops and awards Church of Excellence (COE) Awards. CMT presented COE Awards to 14 churches at the 2025 Annual Conference and received almost 20 applications for 2026. Clergy Co-chair: Anjie Peek Rivers; Lay Co-chair: Lee D. Highsmith.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 301 (Connectional Ministries Team Report)

title: Connectional Ministries – Advocacy Committee
summary: The Advocacy Committee pledged to "amplify advocacy" in the conference, establishing an advocacy web page and engaging issues including the death penalty, environmental justice, Medicaid, SNAP, poverty, and gun safety.
contentMd: In 2025 the Advocacy Committee pledged to "amplify advocacy" across the North Georgia Conference. It established an advocacy web page (ngumc.org/advocacy) and gave team members access to Church and Society's Building Power Together advocacy toolkit and the 2025 Faith & Facts Cards. The committee participated in GBCS's Grace over Greed webinar and campaign, continued anti-death-penalty awareness (including Georgians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty Day at the Capitol and GFADP's vigil for life), and supported calls to action on environmental justice, Medicaid expansion, SNAP funding, poverty elimination, and gun safety. Chair: Pamela Perkins Carn.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 302 (Connectional Ministries – Advocacy Committee)

title: Conference Commission on Religion and Race
summary: The Conference Commission on Religion and Race (CCORR) works to dismantle systemic racism. It reports a new Facebook page, participation in nominations, the Racial Justice and Healing Academy, reparations work moving to a Committee on Jubilee, and advocacy for an Inclusion and Advocacy staff position.
contentMd:
The Conference Commission on Religion and Race (CCORR) traces its origin to the 1968 establishment of the General Commission on Religion and Race in response to 1960s racial strife, committing to discontinue systemic racism. The commission's 2025 work includes a new Facebook page developed with Connectional Ministries, active participation in the conference nominating process, and the Racial Justice and Healing Academy (RJHA)—work in which North Georgia leads the denomination, requiring participation (and GCORR bias training) to qualify for conference leadership.

The report notes that conference reparations work will transfer, by direction of the bishop, from a task force to a conference Committee on Jubilee, and advocates restoring the Director of Inclusion and Advocacy staff position. It references cabinet agreement to use proceeds from Black church property sales to fund Black Congregational Development grants. Chair: Rev. Dr. Vance P. Ross.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 303 (Conference Commission on Religion and Race)

title: Conference Commission on the Status and Role of Women
summary: COSROW advocates for the full and equal participation of women in the church. It reports an adopted clergy parental leave policy, a clergywomen mentoring program, support for those affected by sexual ethics violations, and the 70th anniversary of women's ordination in the UMC.
contentMd:
The Commission on the Status and Role of Women (COSROW) advocates for the full and equal participation of women in the life and mission of the Church, a task assigned to each annual conference by the Book of Discipline. During annual conference, COSROW volunteers monitor sessions for inclusivity and submit a monitoring report to the conference and General COSROW.

Recent accomplishments include proposing a Parental Leave Policy that the Board of Ordained Ministry adopted, launching a mentoring program pairing clergywomen with experienced colleagues, creating a support system for clergy who have experienced a sexual ethics violation, communicating with the conference salary equalization task force, and developing educational materials to help churches and SPRCs welcome a woman pastor. At this annual conference COSROW celebrates the 70th anniversary of the ordination of women in The United Methodist Church. Representative: Lindsey Solomon.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 304 (Conference Commission on the Status and Role of Women)

title: Disaster Response Ministries
summary: Disaster Response Ministries reports a major UMCOR-led Hurricane Helene recovery effort in the Augusta area, the addition of a Disaster Response Associate, and warehouse/Early Response Team work in partnership with the South Georgia Conference.
contentMd:
Disaster Response Ministries reports growth in congregations partnering with UMCOR. With UMCOR support it added Jamaar Franklin Pye as Disaster Response Associate to help congregations build disaster plans, implement the Connecting Neighbors curriculum, and train Early Response Teams. Grace Lee-Zimmerman leads the Disaster Ministries warehouse at Impact and the MissionHub at the Conference Center, with churches sending groups to assemble UMCOR hygiene and cleaning kits (ngumc.org/warehouse).

A major UMCOR recovery effort has continued in the Augusta area since Hurricane Helene (September 27, 2024), rebuilding homes across a three-county area (Richmond, McDuffie, Columbia). The team received 472 requests for unmet needs and moved 214 projects into case management (as of 3/16/26), securing grant funding from the NGUMC Conference Offering, UMCOR, the Community Foundation of the CSRA, the ELCA Southeastern Synod, and the American Red Cross. Volunteer hours peaked at 342 volunteers working 13,403 hours in January 2026. Over 100 homes were repaired or rebuilt in the past year. Submitted by Scott Parrish.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 305 (Disaster Response Ministries)

title: Global Ministries & UMVIM
summary: The Conference Secretaries of Global Ministries report that 19 North Georgia churches sent UMVIM mission teams internationally in 2025, and North Georgia giving to Global Ministries and UMCOR was nearly $518,000.
contentMd:
Global Ministries & United Methodist Volunteers in Mission (UMVIM) report that in 2025, 19 North Georgia churches sent mission teams in coordination with UMVIM to partner destinations including Belize, Brazil, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Kenya, and Nicaragua, increasingly using best practices like international team insurance.

North Georgia giving to the General Board of Global Ministries (GBGM) and UMCOR in 2025 was almost $518,000, supporting 18 missionaries directly and over 200 missionaries serving in 60 countries, plus denominational disaster relief. GBGM's Feeding Our Neighbors food grants supported UMC-affiliated food banks and pantries. Current opportunities include serving at the Disaster Ministries warehouse/MissionHub and sending teams to the Augusta Hurricane Helene recovery. Conference Secretaries of Global Ministries: AnnaKate Rawles and Scott Parrish.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 306 (Global Ministries & UMVIM)

title: Aldersgate Homes & Camp Collinswood
summary: Aldersgate Homes serves the disabilities community through advocacy, education, and recreation, including the accessible Collinswood retreat center on Lake Oconee. It is hosting the Annual Conference "We Are Able" 5K and marks 35 years of ministry.
contentMd:
Aldersgate Homes/Collinswood serves the disabilities community in North Georgia through advocacy, education, and recreation, working with churches and individuals to create welcoming communities for people of all abilities. Its Collinswood retreat center on Lake Oconee offers fully accessible cottages, a dining/meeting hall, pavilion, boathouse, gazebo, and dock, used in 2025 for confirmation, youth, and adult retreats. The Marian Wilder Award recognizes churches that create accessible programs and facilities.

Aldersgate Homes is hosting the Annual Conference "We Are Able" 5K on Saturday, June 20 at 7 a.m., with proceeds supporting its ministry; a conference-wide offering is held in October. The report gives thanks for 35 years of support. Submitted by Lindsey Solomon.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 400 (Aldersgate Homes and Collinswood)

title: Methodist Foundation for Retired Ministers
summary: The Methodist Foundation for Retired Ministers maintains an endowment to provide for retired ministers and the families of deceased ministers. With its last acquired home sold in 2025, investment income is now its only revenue source.
contentMd:
The Foundation for Retired Ministers maintains a permanent endowment to provide a living for retired ministers, widows, and dependent children of deceased ministers. Historically this was accomplished by acquiring homes for retirees; by the 1970s the conference directed the Foundation to liquidate these homes, and the last home was sold in 2025. The Foundation used some assets to help the conference liquidate the unfunded pre-1982 service liability that benefited retired clergy, and in recent years has funded the Wesley Woods Chaplaincy and assisted individual retirees with disability and health needs not covered elsewhere.

With home sales ended, investment income is now the Foundation's only revenue, requiring careful stewardship as it evaluates how best to meet emerging needs of retired clergy and families. President: David S. Naglee; Executive Director: Ed Tomlinson.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 401 (Methodist Foundation for Retired Ministers)

title: Murphy Harpst
summary: Murphy-Harpst Children's Centers serves vulnerable youth on its Cedartown campus, in Evolve homes, and through foster care. The report describes expanded Evolve and residential programs and the MindVox therapeutic model, with about 20% of its budget from private donations.
contentMd:
Murphy-Harpst Children's Centers has served vulnerable and suffering children for more than a century, supported by congregations across Georgia. About 20% of its operating budget comes from private donations, including the annual Murphy-Harpst Special Offering (launching July 19), which funds therapies not covered by state funding. Georgia's foster care system serves nearly twice as many children as there are licensed foster homes, and the state relies on Murphy-Harpst for adolescents with higher clinical needs.

In the past year, the community-based Evolve Initiative expanded to serve 28 youth, with nearly 90% showing measurable behavioral-health improvement. The Cedartown campus serves about 80 youth and opened a second Qualified Residential Treatment Program, achieving an 81% success rate transitioning youth to family or other settings. The clinical team's MindVox model integrates music and songwriting with Cognitive Behavior Therapy to help youth process trauma. President & CEO: Michael S. Merritt.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 402 (Murphy-Harpst Children's Centers)

title: North Georgia Camp & Retreat Ministries
summary: North Georgia Camp & Retreat Ministries (NGCRM) focuses on helping campers discover they are loved children of God. Glisson retreat ministries grew slightly in 2025 (8,430 guests), while camp attendance declined 2%.
contentMd:
North Georgia Camp & Retreat Ministries (NGCRM) centers its work on helping participants discover their "why"—affirming campers as loved and gifted children of God as a foundation for faith and calling. In 2025, Glisson's retreat ministries grew slightly with 8,430 guests; just under 25% of retreat groups were from United Methodist churches or ministries, and overall retreat attendance increased slightly from a record 2024.

Camp attendance declined by 2% in 2025, with Glisson enrollment down 78 campers. Grow Day Camps served 655 campers at 19 partner sites, and ELI grew to 57 high-school juniors and seniors; 38% of 2025 summer campers were members of United Methodist congregations (down from 41% in 2024 and 49% in 2023). Over the next 2–3 years NGCRM plans to deepen partnerships with camper parents and families. Chairperson: Bill Martin; Executive Director: C. Russell Davis.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 403 (North Georgia Camp and Retreat Ministries, Inc.)

title: Wellroot Family Services
summary: Wellroot Family Services, the United Methodist Children's Home in North Georgia for 155 years, reports impacting 3,843 lives in Fiscal Year 2025 through family therapy, new-mother support, foster care, and trauma training, supported by 186 churches.
contentMd:
Wellroot Family Services, the United Methodist Children's Home in North Georgia for 155 years, leads with care—beginning every conversation not with "what did you do" but "what happened to you?" In Fiscal Year 2025, 3,843 lives were impacted: 620 children, teens, parents, and siblings worked together through Functional Family Therapy; 670 new mothers and babies received early support; 120 parents gained parenting skills; 121 young adults and families found stability; 156 children found caring homes through community partners; 105 children and teens experienced nurturing foster families; and 1,931 teachers, social workers, and community leaders were equipped to understand trauma.

186 churches showed up with compassion to support this work. Wellroot especially thanks its top five giving churches: Dunwoody UMC, Peachtree Road UMC, Northside UMC, St. James UMC Atlanta, and Johns Creek UMC. President & CEO: F. Allison Ashe.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 404 (Wellroot Family Services)

title: Wesley Woods
summary: Wesley Woods creates communities of connection, well-being, and promise for older adults. In the past year it provided more than $1,400,000 in rent or meal assistance and chaplains made more than 12,000 connections with residents and families.
contentMd:
Wesley Woods' mission is to create communities of connection, well-being, and promise for older adults, which it has done for 72 years with support from the Mother's Day Offering, church budgets, and endowments. Noting that older adults are the fastest-growing segment of the homeless population, Wesley Woods provided more than $1,400,000 in rent or meal assistance this past year to residents who outlived their resources or needed help with higher levels of care.

Chaplains in each community offer pastoral care—worship, Bible study, prayer groups, and choirs—providing more than 12,000 connections with residents, families, and care partners last year. Wellness programming helps residents remain in independent living longer, and the Masterful Moments program builds dementia-care empathy and skills among staff. President & CEO: Terry Barcroft; Foundation President: Diane Vaughan.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 405 (Wesley Woods)

title: Conference Board of Laity
summary: Conference Lay Leader Kim Powell reflects on two years of service, the Board of Laity's district training events, and work on the One Georgia Task Force toward conference unification.
contentMd:
Conference Lay Leader Kim Powell reflects on two years of service, grounding the Board of Laity's work in the 2026 theme "Unto the least of these" and Philippians 2:1–5. The Board—including United Women in Faith, United Methodist Men, the UM Council on Scouting, Lay Servant Ministries, District Lay Leaders, and Associate Conference Lay Leaders—held training events and worship in each district, meeting at Peachtree Road UMC and Ben Hill UMC.

Powell served with her South Georgia counterpart Scott Cleaveland on the One Georgia Task Force, traveling the state on projects including the 2025 One Georgia Advent Devotional, the Sacred Spaces Devotional, the One Georgia Unification Report, and town hall meetings to educate members about becoming the Georgia Conference.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 500 (Conference Board of Laity)

title: Lay Servant Ministries
summary: Lay Servant Ministries equips laity for leading, communicating, and caring. In 2025 the conference had 74 Certified Lay Speakers and over 400 Certified Lay Servants, who provided over 458 pulpit fills.
contentMd:
Lay Servant Ministries, framed by Book of Discipline ¶¶266–269, equips laity for Leading, Communicating, and Caring ministries. In 2025 the conference had 74 Certified Lay Speakers and over 400 Certified Lay Servants. Seventy-four individuals began the journey by registering for one of 16 Basic courses, with 397 total class registrations; 71 classes (basic and advanced) were offered, 62 in person or on Zoom and 9 in a self-paced Google Classroom format. Beyond the six required advanced courses for Lay Speaker certification, many additional advanced courses were offered.

Certified Lay Speakers provided over 458 pulpit fills for Sundays when clergy needed time away, and Lay Servants served in caring, outreach, and home-church ministries throughout the conference. Conference Director: Mary Williams.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 501 (Lay Servant Ministries)

title: Order of Deaconess & Home Missioner
summary: The Order of Deaconess/Home Missioner continues a legacy of love, justice, and service. North Georgia has eleven active and three retired Deaconess/Home Missioners serving under appointment.
contentMd:
The Order of Deaconess/Home Missioner roots its work in Romans 16:1–2 and the deaconess movement begun by Lucy Rider Meyer, whose first training school opened in Chicago in 1885; the Office of Deaconess was officially recognized by the General Conference in 1888. Deaconesses and Home Missioners continue this legacy of serving in cutting-edge ministries of love, justice, and service.

The North Georgia Conference has eleven active Deaconess/Home Missioners serving under appointment and three in retired relationship, plus one active and one retired Deaconess from other conferences living within its bounds. Their ministries this year included counseling those facing economic or immigration hardship, senior home health services, food-insecurity efforts, and advocacy against injustice. One retired North Georgia DHM represents the Order in DIAKONIA, the international ecumenical diaconal community, which gathered in Tanzania in July 2025 and celebrated the consecration of 15 Africa Region deaconess/home missioners. Submitted by L. Susan Stroup.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 502 (Order of Deaconess/Home Missioner)

title: Scouting Ministry
summary: The North Georgia UM Committee on Scouting supports Scouting as a church ministry, focusing on starting and maintaining Scout units and encouraging faith-based programs. It hosted the Bishop's Scout Lunch in September 2025 with 50+ churches attending.
contentMd:
The North Georgia United Methodist Committee on Scouting (UMCOS) supports Scouting in the church—Boy Scout, Girl Scout, and Big Brother Big Sister programs—through two objectives: (1) starting and maintaining new Scouting units at churches, and (2) encouraging faith-based programs such as the P.R.A.Y. Christian education program. It provides advisory and training services to help clergy and leaders make Scouting a vibrant congregational ministry.

A major 2025 event was the Bishop's Scout Lunch on September 25, 2025, attended by 50-plus churches from all districts along with partners from GSUSA and Scouting America; Jai Ferrell, CEO of the Girl Scouts of Greater Atlanta Council, addressed the gathering. Scout Coordinator: Chris Karabinos.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 503 (North Georgia United Methodist Committee on Scouting)

title: North Georgia United Methodist Men
summary: North Georgia United Methodist Men reports on its purpose and covenant, the outgoing president's final term, and goals for 2026–2027 including increasing charters. It notes about 20% of roughly 440 churches contribute dues and is working toward One Georgia consolidation.
contentMd:
North Georgia United Methodist Men describes itself as a creative, supportive fellowship of men declaring the centrality of Christ, abiding by the UMM Purpose & Covenant. Outgoing Conference President Ernest Perry concludes his fourth and final term. North and South Georgia UMM leadership are working with Bishop Dease and the General Commission on UMM toward One Georgia consolidation, with a formal merger vote to occur at both conferences.

The report notes that only about 20% of roughly 440 churches contribute dues—approximately 82 churches at the national level and 18 charters at the conference level. Goals for 2026–2027 include increasing active charters from 82 to 100 (national) and 18 to 60 (conference), hosting an in-person UMM retreat in August, raising $2,000 for North Georgia men's ministries, and identifying five district presidents. President: Ernest Perry.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 504 (North Georgia United Methodist Men)

title: United Women in Faith
summary: North Georgia United Women in Faith reports a year of growth, discipleship, and impact under the theme "Acting Boldly, Practicing Hope, Showing Up, Making a Difference," with district retreats, Mission U, racial justice work, and planning for One Georgia unification.
contentMd:
North Georgia United Women in Faith (UWFaith) reports a year of growth, discipleship, and impact under the theme "Acting Boldly, Practicing Hope, Showing Up, Making a Difference" (Ephesians 2:10), pursuing goals of welcoming sisterhood, increased mission pledges, and community impact. Each district hosted a Lenten Day Apart; the Spiritual Growth/Social Action Retreat met May 2–3, 2025, at Pinnacle Retreat Center, and Soul Care 2026 gathered nearly 150 people. Mission U 2025 included an Ubuntu service project assembling more than 250 Care Kits and 150 Menstrual Kits.

UWFaith continued supporting its four National Mission Institutions (New Bethlehem Community Center, Paine College, Murphy-Harpst, and Clark Atlanta University) and advanced racial justice through a study of Jemar Tisby's The Color of Compromise and a screening of the film Pushout with Clark Atlanta University. More than ninety members registered for Assembly 2026 in Indianapolis. A team of twenty-one leaders (eleven from North Georgia, ten from South Georgia) is planning for potential One Georgia unification. President: Jessica Godfrey.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 505 (North Georgia United Women in Faith)

title: Black Methodists for Church Renewal
summary: The North Georgia Caucus of Black Methodists for Church Renewal (NGBMCR) supports Black churches in the conference through town halls, the Hush Arbor, a Camp Glisson scholarship program, and participation in CCORR and the Reparations Task Force.
contentMd:
Black Methodists for Church Renewal (BMCR) is the organized Black caucus of The United Methodist Church, one of five official U.S.-based ethnic caucuses, representing more than 2,400 Black UM congregations and approximately 500,000 African American members denomination-wide. In 2025 the North Georgia caucus (NGBMCR) held pre- and post-Annual Conference town halls to assess the impact of structural and legislative changes on Black churches, continued its "Getting to Know NGBMCR" visitation initiative, and offered the NGBMCR Hush Arbor (a seventh year) as a space for prayer, meditation, and fellowship at the 2025 Annual Conference.

NGBMCR engaged children and youth through a Camp Glisson scholarship program, participated in CCORR and the conference Reparations Task Force, held quarterly membership meetings, sent a letter to Emory's interim president objecting to elimination of DEI programming, and submitted a Black History Month presentation. Chair: Pamela Perkins Carn.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 600 (Black Methodists for Church Renewal - North Georgia Caucus)

title: Drew University Theological School
summary: Drew University Theological School is a global seminary educating leaders for the worldwide church. In Fall 2025 it welcomed 88 new students for a total headcount of 365, including 140 international students.
contentMd:
Drew University Theological School is a global seminary serving the worldwide church, building on its Wesleyan and Methodist foundations and offering in-person classes in Madison, New Jersey, fully online and hybrid classes, and an in-person Doctor of Ministry program in South Korea. In Fall 2025 Drew welcomed 88 new students for a total headcount of 365, with strong international enrollment of 140 students.

Its interdisciplinary programs emphasize real-world apprenticeships, adaptive leadership, and team-taught core courses, infused with the faculty's shared values: anti-racism, gender and sexual-identity equality, eco-sustainability and environmental justice, and interfaith understanding. Drew continues to experience an increase in United Methodist students, including UM Global Fellows, with graduates serving across the connection. Dean: Edwin David Aponte.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 601 (Drew University Theological School)

title: Duke University Divinity School
summary: Duke Divinity School celebrated its 99th Opening Convocation in 2025 and commemorated the 1700th anniversary of the Nicene Creed. It welcomed 219 new students, including 120 in the Master of Divinity program (10% growth), and four new faculty.
contentMd:
Duke Divinity School celebrated its 99th Opening Convocation in August 2025 with a sermon by Dean Edgardo Colón-Emeric launching a Nicene Creed Preaching Series. Joining Christians worldwide to commemorate the 1700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea, Duke scholars published Trinitarian Matters: 1700 Years of Shaping Christian Identity and Practice and hosted two conference events exploring Nicaea.

In 2025 Duke welcomed 219 new students, including 120 in the Master of Divinity program (10% growth), plus new students across MA in Christian Practice (6), Doctor of Ministry (34), Master of Theology (7), Master of Theological Studies (32), Doctor of Theology (5), and the Certificate in Theology and Health Care (14). Duke confirmed an MOU with Huntingdon College and welcomed four new faculty. Dean: Edgardo Colón-Emeric.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 602 (Duke Divinity School)

title: Garrett-Evangelical Theological Seminary
summary: Garrett-Evangelical reports a fifth consecutive year of enrollment growth, the launch of The Garrett Collective digital learning platform, and a historic agreement with Northwestern University to relocate to new campus facilities.
contentMd:
Garrett-Evangelical Theological Seminary reports continued growth, innovation, and partnership rooted in its Wesleyan heritage. For the fifth consecutive year it welcomed an entering class reflecting sustained enrollment growth, with students from across the U.S. and more than twenty countries preparing for ministry in congregations, chaplaincy, nonprofits, academia, and mission.

Garrett launched The Garrett Collective, a comprehensive digital platform offering theological resources, courses, and stackable microcredentials in multiple languages, developed in partnership with annual conferences and congregations. The seminary announced a historic agreement with longtime campus partner Northwestern University to relocate to new state-of-the-art facilities on the southern end of campus, supporting its multi-modal student body. Grant support has strengthened initiatives including the Center for Ecological Regeneration, spiritual-formation and Hispanic pastoral-leadership programs, and a Mageto Fellows Program in partnership with Africa University. President: Javier A. Viera.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 603 (Garrett-Evangelical Theological Seminary)

title: Georgia UM Colleges, Universities & Wesley Foundations
summary: This report compiles campus-ministry highlights from Georgia's United Methodist colleges, universities, and Wesley Foundations, including worship, discipleship, mission trips, and community service across roughly twenty campuses.
contentMd:
This composite report gathers campus religious-life highlights from Georgia's United Methodist colleges, universities, and Wesley Foundations. Examples include: Andrew College launching weekly Monday worship; Clark Atlanta University welcoming its largest, highest-GPA freshman class and hosting a Pushout film dialogue with UWFaith; Columbus State Wesley hiring its first "homegrown" intern; Emory Chaplains' "Beloved Community" worship and WISE pre-orientation; and Emory Wesley re-establishing its Wesley Fellowship in January 2026.

Further highlights: Georgia Gwinnett College Wesley building 70 beds with Sleep in Heavenly Peace; Georgia Southern's Civil Rights Pilgrimage to Selma and Montgomery; Georgia Tech Wesley's facility renovations; Kennesaw State Wesley partnerships with St. Paul UMC and Murphy Harpst; LaGrange College students rebuilding homes in Savannah; Paine College's growing Wesley Fellowship; Reinhardt's first international mission trip to Peru and its "22 Initiative"; UGA Wesley sending 198 students to Jamaica and 40 to Cuba; West Georgia Wesley's "Sweet Tea Tuesdays"; Valdosta State Wesley's residential community; the Wesley Foundation of Macon's Backpack Buddies ministry; Wesleyan College hosting the South Georgia Annual Conference opening worship; and Young Harris College launching a campus food pantry serving over 900 people.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 604 (Georgia United Methodist Colleges, Universities, and Wesley Foundations)

title: United Theological Seminary
summary: United Theological Seminary, founded in 1871, served 642 graduate students in 2024-25, reflecting about 30% enrollment growth since 2021. It introduced a Doctor of Theology degree and reports President Kent Millard's retirement effective June 30, 2026.
contentMd:
United Theological Seminary, founded in 1871, served 642 graduate students (275 doctoral, 375 master's) in the 2024-25 fiscal year—approximately 30% enrollment growth since 2021—placing it among the largest United Methodist seminaries. Students came from 38 states, 24 nations, and 54 denominations, with United Methodists the largest denominational group. United introduced a Doctor of Theology in 2024 (13 students in its first year); its Doctor of Ministry program enrolled 262 mentor-led students, and master's programs span eight houses of study (offered in English, Spanish, and Korean), including new African and Hispanic Houses of Study.

The Fresh Wind Campaign to raise $10 million for the endowment has raised more than $9 million. President Kent Millard announced his retirement effective June 30, 2026, after ten years; a Presidential Search Committee is identifying his successor, who will begin July 1, 2026.
source: 2026 NGC Handbook — report 605 (United Theological Seminary)
